transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-09-07 
Time: 15:00 UTC 
Duration: 54 minutes 
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Park (Redwood SE), Lina Gomez (Redwood CSM), Jared Lowe (Crestfall Head of Platform), Priya Nair (Crestfall ML Eng), Marcus Holt (Crestfall CTO)

Summary (auto): Demo of model catalog flows; show how Console + API + Optimize help pick open models, run interpretation on bench results, and choose runtime-compatible kernels. Discussed quantization profiles, routing fallbacks, and security posture for VPC/private deploys.

--- Transcript start ---
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh, we'll run about 45 to 55 minutes today, want to walk through the catalog narrowing flow then jump into the bench interpretation. Ethan is going to show the kernel map in the console and Lina will drop the security docs at the end.
[00:14] Jared Lowe: Sounds good, thanks Maya. We're mainly trying to see how Redwood helps us pick an open model that hits our latency and cost targets, but we also have to keep everything within our VPC for regulatory reasons. So, privacy is a hard constraint.
[00:26] Ethan Park: Totally. We'll show both hosted and private flow, and highlight what changes for dedicated / on-prem. Quick question: what's your target p95 latency for the convo path?
[00:34] Priya Nair: Target is p95 below 150 milliseconds for single-turn generation at ~1k token window. Realistic load is 120 TPS peak but bursts to 300 for short windows.
[00:45] Ethan Park: Great — that helps frame batching and kernel choices. Quick note: some of our console labels get munged in transcription, you might see "Red Wood Optimize" in places. It's same thing, it's Redwood Optimize.
[00:58] Marcus Holt: Also cost target, ballpark: under $0.20 per 1k tokens *served* ideally. If quant helps meet latency but increases hallucinations that's a tradeoff we need to see.
[01:09] Maya Chen: Okay perfect. We'll start with the catalog UI — for folks who haven't used it, it surfaces curated open models with fit scores, bench metrics, and a compatibility matrix indicating kernel and hardware mappings.
[01:21] Ethan Park: (screen share) Alright, console: left nav -> Catalog -> Shortlist. Here we've prefiltered by family (decoder-only open models) and by your latency bucket. See the fit score on the right, which is a weighted aggregation of bench signal (latency, perf variance), task fit (our evals for instruction-following), and cost index.
[01:37] Jared Lowe: That fit score — is it tunable? Say Priya cares 2x more about hallucination rate than latency, can we change weights?
[01:45] Ethan Park: Yes, Optimize lets you set your objective profile. If you flip to a quality-first profile the score reweights and the shortlist reshuffles. Also you can pin metrics you care about and exclude models that don't meet a threshold.
[01:56] Priya Nair: Great. Can you show how bench signals are interpreted? We saw raw numbers but want a human-readable summary.
[02:03] Ethan Park: Sure. Open the bench results for the "shortlist run" we prepared — you'll see the top chart is latency distribution, second is regeneration quality delta against baseline, third is cost per 1k tokens, and below that, compatibility notes: quantization tolerance, kernel mapping (cuda xla? we sometimes label things slightly differently), and memory pressure.
[02:22] [02:22] Speaker 1: So the bench shows Model A with median 90ms but p95 spikes to 220ms under batching, Model B 120ms median p95 140ms but higher cost.
[02:33] Ethan Park: Exactly, and the console flags models where batching interactions will likely blow p95 because the runtime's continuous batching heuristics look at request size distribution you uploaded. If your 95th is single-turn small messages, we can tune batching to prioritize latency.
[02:48] Priya Nair: We upload traces? Is there a template?
[02:51] Maya Chen: Yes, we'll share the workload template—Priya you can paste sanitized traces into the bench job and we run it with your token distribution. That way the compatibility matrix is grounded in your real workload.
[03:03] Marcus Holt: I want to understand kernel mapping — you mentioned a magic mapping to hardware kernels. Explain that a bit more.
[03:09] Ethan Park: Sure — behind the scenes the runtime picks optimized kernels and memory layouts based on model architecture, sequence length and quantized dtype (int8/int4). The compatibility matrix shows which kernels we recommend (e.g., fused-attn-opt, kv-compact, int8-llm-kernel-v2) and whether those kernels are available on the target GPU family. If a recommended kernel isn't available on your private fleet, the console suggests fallbacks and shows perf delta estimates.
[03:33] [03:33] Maya Chen: Quick caveat, those fallback deltas are estimates from our microbench corpus — the actual delta depends on your real input shapes, that's why bench runs are important.
[03:44] Priya Nair: For quantization, how do you show quality regression? We don't want to blindly trust a single metric.
[03:50] Ethan Park: We show a breakdown: instruction-following scores, factual accuracy probes, and a small hallucination suite. You can upload your own eval set too. When quantizing we run both int8 and int4 profiles with a per-prompt quality delta and an "alert threshold" you set — if delta exceeds threshold we mark it in red and recommend keeping higher precision or exploring mixed-precision output layers.
[04:11] Jared Lowe: Do we get the raw delta logs? Our QA wants to inspect examples where quantization caused regressions.
[04:16] Ethan Park: Yes, the bench artifact includes example traces for failed prompts and raw logits; we can share those logs. Bear in mind some tokenization mismatches show up in transcripts, but we include token-level diffs.
[04:28] [04:28] Speaker 2: (muffled) Are prompts pinned during rollouts?
[04:31] Lina Gomez: Yes, rollout policies let you pin a set of canary prompts and/or user segments. Console supports canary -> A/B -> full rollout paths and auto-fallback if quality drift crosses a threshold. You can tie that to traffic weights or specific API keys.
[04:45] Priya Nair: Speaking of API keys, how do we handle secrets in a private VPC? We use HSM/KMS in-house.
[04:51] Maya Chen: For Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. Keys never leave your control plane. For hosted we support Redwood-managed KMS with FIPS options and we have options for customer-supplied KMS in Dedicated.
[05:03] Marcus Holt: SOC2 and auditing — we need audit logs and SSO.
[05:07] Lina Gomez: We will send SOC2 docs and audit log examples; console has per-request tracing and token-level attribution. SSO via SAML/Okta supported, and RBAC is fine-grained. We'll email the compliance pack after the call.
[05:20] Ethan Park: Back to selection flow — once you pick 2-3 models from the shortlist, Redwood Optimize suggests quantization profiles + batching configs per model and an expected cost/latency corridor. That suggestion includes a recommended kernel mapping for your target hardware.
[05:36] Jared Lowe: Can you show a sample Optimize suggestion?
[05:39] Ethan Park: (navigates) Here's an example: Model C — suggestion: int8 + KV cache warmup 2-step, batch size cap 8, continuous batching window 10ms, recommended kernel: fused-attn-opt-v3, expected p95 130ms on A100-80GB equiv; cost estimate $0.16/1k tokens. There's a confidence band and sensitivity curve showing how p95 changes if percent small requests increases.
[06:02] Priya Nair: The sensitivity curve is useful — can Optimize ingest our latency SLO and automatically prioritize a policy?
[06:07] Ethan Park: Yes, you can generate an objective profile: latency-first, cost-capped, or custom weights. Optimize will then generate multiple candidate configs and a Pareto frontier so you can pick a run that trades cost vs latency vs quality.
[06:19] [06:19] Speaker 3: How do we deploy multiple model variants for routing?
[06:22] Ethan Park: We support multi-variant routing. Policy can be region-based, SLO-based (latency buckets), or cost-tier fallback. For example, warm traffic goes to Model C int8 variant and overflow to Model B fp16 variant in a higher-capacity pool. The routing layer monitors tail latency and can shift weights automatically.
[06:39] Marcus Holt: If we go Private, does Redwood still provide the control plane? We need everything under our VPC.
[06:45] Maya Chen: For Private we offer a customer-controlled control plane with optional managed services. You can elect to host the control plane in your VPC or use our control plane with a private connector. Sensitive metering and logs can be kept in your account.
[06:58] Priya Nair: Quick follow: if we host the control plane, do you still ship kernel updates?
[07:03] Ethan Park: We ship runtime updates as artifacts; your ops team can choose to approve and apply them. For high-security customers we do a packaging flow with release notes and signed binaries.
[07:13] [07:13] Speaker 1: (laughs) Good to know.
[07:16] Jared Lowe: Okay, let's walk a concrete example — our starting shortlist is five open models you preselected. Can you show the decision path from five to final two given our SLOs?
[07:26] Ethan Park: Sure — step 1: filter by architecture and license. Step 2: run a lightweight bench with your traces to get latency/cost/quality deltas. Step 3: consult Optimize to generate quant profiles and kernel mappings. Step 4: check compatibility matrix for your target hardware and flag any kernel gaps. Step 5: run a focused bench on candidate variants (int8, int4, fp16) and inspect per-prompt deltas. Step 6: pick 1-2 candidates and run a pilot.
[07:57] [07:57] Priya Nair: In that step 4, what constitutes a kernel gap? For example, if a fused-attn kernel isn't available on our older fleet of V100s, what do you do?
[08:05] Ethan Park: We would surface it as a gap and provide the fallback kernel path and a perf delta estimate. For V100s you might see 30-60% slower p95 for that architecture versus newer Ampere or Hopper kernels. We can also recommend a quantization profile that is more conservative to reduce mem pressure and avoid OOMs.
[08:23] Maya Chen: Also worth pointing out the console has a hardware compatibility matrix that maps model family -> recommended kernel -> supported GPU families. You can export that matrix as CSV to feed into ops.
[08:36] Jared Lowe: Exportable, good. We'll feed that into our procurement/ops sheet.
[08:40] [08:40] Speaker 2: Any examples of hallucination regressions with int4?
[08:43] Ethan Park: We saw a few models where int4 increased hallucination on long-context summarization tasks. That's why the bench includes a targeted hallucination probe. For those models Optimize will often recommend mixed-precision — keep embeddings and early layers fp16, quantize later layers — to balance quality and perf.
[09:00] Priya Nair: How do Rollouts handle user-level personalization? We can't risk breaking power users.
[09:06] Lina Gomez: Rollouts can be scoped by user segment and API key. You can keep a safe cohort (power users) excluded from the canary and monitor quality metrics. If drift occurs, automatic rollback triggers.
[09:17] [09:17] Maya Chen: Quick note on billing: hosted usage pricing is token-based; Dedicated gives committed pricing with burst buckets. For Private we have platform licensing plus support. We'll share a rough pricing estimator for your target QPS.
[09:32] Jared Lowe: On the bench run — can we simulate our burst profile (120 -> 300 TPS)? We want to see p95 under realistic spikes.
[09:39] Ethan Park: Yes, bench supports stepped load profiles and can simulate cold/warm cache patterns for KV caching. We can inject burst windows and produce latency heatmaps.
[09:50] Priya Nair: KV cache — we use a custom cache invalidation pattern, will that break anything?
[09:55] Ethan Park: It depends. The runtime exposes hooks for cache eviction and we can adapt policies. If you have nonstandard invalidation, we'll test it in the bench. Sometimes you see cache churn causing degraded p95; we can recommend cache TTL and warmup strategies.
[10:08] [10:08] Speaker 3: A few quick objections from Procurement: vendor lock-in, and open-model licensing. How do you handle model provenance?
[10:15] Maya Chen: We surface license metadata in the catalog and flag models with restrictive terms. For vendor lock-in, our SDKs and API are model-agnostic; you can export model artifacts and the config manifests. For Private deployments, artifacts stay in your registry.
[10:29] Marcus Holt: Can you demo exporting a config and a small manifest?
[10:33] Ethan Park: (screen) Sure — from the shortlist you can click "export manifest" — it gives you a YAML that includes model name/version, chosen quant profile, kernel hints, hardware pinned labels, and rollout policy. You can check it into your infra repo or hand to ops for on-prem deployment.
[10:50] Priya Nair: About the short-listing heuristics — can we add a custom metric? For us, inference determinism matters for reproducibility checks.
[10:58] Ethan Park: Yes, you can add custom metrics via the console in the "Metrics" tab and upload a custom evaluator. That metric will be included in the fit score if you opt in.
[11:10] [11:10] Maya Chen: Jumping ahead — bench artifacts we provide include raw logs, perf counters, and token-level deltas. We'll make sure you get those for QA.
[11:19] Jared Lowe: Excellent. I want to call out one operational constraint: all logs must be kept on-prem for 12 months for compliance. Can Redwood do that?
[11:28] Lina Gomez: Yes, for Private we can configure log retention to be local and meet your retention policy. We'll provide a runbook for archiving logs to your S3-equivalent in the VPC.
[11:39] Priya Nair: One more question — latency attribution. How do we separate client-side vs server-side latency in bench?
[11:44] Ethan Park: Bench reports both; it runs a simulated client and emits client-timestamps plus server trace. We also instrument tokenization overhead separately so you can see where time is spent.
[11:55] [11:55] Speaker 2: Does Optimize recommend batching windows automatically?
[11:58] Ethan Park: Yes, Optimize computes an optimal batching window based on your request size distribution and latency SLO. You can auto-apply or review proposals.
[12:08] Maya Chen: Ok, let's run a quick live example: pick model X (open), run a simulated bench on the console with your trace summary and show the compatibility matrix. Ethan, can you run the pre-canned job?
[12:18] Ethan Park: Running now — job queued — we have a lightweight profile that approximates your sample distribution. (pause, typing noises) Results starting to populate; latency histogram up — I'm expanding the compatibility panel.
[12:33] [12:33] Ethan Park: Interesting: Model X int8 median 85ms but p95 190ms; compatibility panel shows fused-attn-opt is available on Ampere and Hopper, but your V100 family hits fallback kernels. It flags a 45% p95 delta on V100.
[12:52] Priya Nair: So on our fleet we'd likely see 200+ ms p95? That's above our SLO.
[12:57] Ethan Park: Correct. Optimize suggests either: 1) choose Model Y (slightly higher cost) with better kernel support on older hardware, or 2) run Model X but use a mixed-precision option. It shows estimated cost differences.
[13:12] Jared Lowe: Walk me through the math for the cost estimate. I'm skeptical about those per-1k numbers.
[13:17] Ethan Park: It's derived from per-token hardware seconds, concurrency, and hourly GPU cost for the chosen pool. For Dedicated/Pri vate we allow you to input your own GPU hourly cost and utilization to get an accurate number. The console uses our default as a baseline.
[13:32] [13:32] Speaker 1: Are benchmarks deterministic? If we re-run will results change a lot?
[13:36] Ethan Park: We aim for low variance — microbench and multiple repeats give confidence bands. Variance can come from scheduling noise, network jitter, or warm cache. We surface confidence intervals on each metric.
[13:47] Priya Nair: If we choose Model Y, will any pre-trained adapters or LoRA we apply be included in the compatibility matrix?
[13:54] Ethan Park: Good question. Small adapters are supported; if you plan to attach custom LoRA or adapters, include them in the bench run as part of the artifact. Kernels assume base model structure; significant architecture changes can affect kernel selection and we'll rerun kernel heuristics against the adapter-injected model.
[14:11] [14:11] Maya Chen: We're at about 14 minutes — still got a lot to cover but good signal so far. Ethan, can you highlight the CSV export for ops and the manifest again?
[14:20] Ethan Park: (click) Export -> CSV gives model, quant profile, kernel hint, hardware compatibility boolean, estimated p95, estimated cost/1k. Manifest is more detailed and includes rollout policy.
[14:33] Jared Lowe: One more procurement point — SLA on dedicated pools, is that negotiable?
[14:39] Lina Gomez: We have standard SLA tiers for Dedicated. For enterprise we can negotiate specific uptime and latency SLOs tied to committed capacity. We'll include SLA options in the quote.
[14:50] Priya Nair: How long does a typical bench run take for our dataset? We need to plan a 2-week pilot.
[14:56] Ethan Park: Lightweight bench ~ a few hours; full fidelity runs with stepped load and multiple repeats take 1-2 days per model variant. For the pilot we'll run a parallelized suite across 2-3 variants and deliver results in under two weeks.
[15:09] [15:09] Speaker 3: Any references or case studies for similar customers?
[15:12] Maya Chen: We'll share a short case study where a customer moved from an initial shortlist to a dominated model that reduced cost 28% while keeping p95 below target by switching to mixed precision and the right kernel. I'll include that in the follow-up email.
[15:25] Jared Lowe: Sounds good. I'm worried about int4 — if quality slips for our summarization use-case, is there a quick rollback path?
[15:31] Ethan Park: Yes, rollout policies include immediate rollback on an automated quality check; you can also throttle traffic and divert to a higher-precision fallback pool.
[15:40] [15:40] Priya Nair: Okay, let's capture what we need: we'll share traces and SLO doc, you run a bench with int8/int4 + mixed profiles, and then we reconvene with the detailed bench artifacts.
[15:51] Maya Chen: Correct. Next steps we'll put in the CRM. Lina will send SOC2 and VPC docs. I'll upload the shortlist export and preliminary cost estimator.
[15:59] Marcus Holt: When do you need our final decision for Q4 planning? We need to know procurement implications.
[16:04] Maya Chen: If you want production by end of Q4, we recommend starting the pilot this month and locking Dedicated or Private procurement by mid-October. We'll put a timeline in the follow-up.
[16:15] [16:15] Jared Lowe: Great. Any final questions from Crestfall?
[16:18] Priya Nair: No, that's it for now. Thanks.
[16:21] Marcus Holt: Thanks everyone.
[16:24] Maya Chen: Alright we'll wrap — recap and next steps in email. Thanks all.
[16:28] [END OF TRANSCRIPT — automatic ending note: call ended at 16:54 UTC per recorder]

Notes about transcription quality: occasional mislabels and filler words; product names sometimes split as "Red Wood". Multiple references to exports and bench artifacts which Redwood will provide as links in follow-up.
